title: Projects Are a Different Animal

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Shop floor at night, pallets of LED retrofit kits staged by a project trailer. Kyle in front of the pallets, medium shot.
scenes.says: Most of what you've trained on so far is service work. Something's broken, you find out why, you fix it. A project is different. The answer is already known before you leave the shop. Someone surveyed the building, picked the material and promised the customer a result, a schedule and a price. Your job is to deliver that promise, the same way, hundreds of times in a row.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Split screen. Left: a tech at one dark fixture in an office, asking the contact questions, metering, finding a failed driver, packing up an hour later. Right: the same tech on a 600-fixture retrofit's first night, meeting the site contact, counting cartons against the paperwork. Kyle voice-over.
scenes.on_screen:
Service call: a puzzle with one unknown
Project: deliver what was promised
scenes.says: Same tech, two days. On the left, a service call. A puzzle with one unknown. She asks questions, meters, finds a failed driver and leaves in an hour. On the right, the first night of a 600-fixture retrofit. She meets the site contact, checks the material count against the paperwork, sets up a cart line, takes before photos and starts a daily recap.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Kyle back on the shop floor, medium close-up.
scenes.on_screen: Troubleshooting rewards curiosity. Projects reward planning.
scenes.says: Great troubleshooters sometimes struggle on their first projects. That's not a skill problem. It's a gear problem. Troubleshooting rewards curiosity and improvising. Projects reward planning, repetition, communication and paperwork. Good senior techs learn to shift gears on purpose.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Close-up of a printed project specifics sheet on a clipboard with a survey attached.
scenes.on_screen: "Tech, read me before you leave the shop."
scenes.says: Here's what we've learned across a lot of projects. The more details the crew had before kickoff, the better the first night went. When details had to be discovered on site, the job lost hours on day one and often never caught up. That's why every project comes with a specifics sheet. For years it started with: Tech, read me before you leave the shop.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Right-side footage continues: cart line feeding lifts, a tech counting cartons, another taking a photo, the recap being typed.
scenes.on_screen: Read before you roll | Plan the flow | Repeat the same good install | Count everything | Write it down | Talk early | Be the professional
scenes.says: The project mindset. Read before you roll. Plan the flow, not just the fixture. Repeat the same good install, because consistency is the product. Count everything: in, installed, left over, removed. Write it down and take the picture. Talk early, because a shortage on day one is small and on the last day it's large. And be the lighting professional on site.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Night retrofit: two lifts in an aisle, a tech applying a lock and tag at a panel.
scenes.on_screen: Safety rules don't relax on repetitive work
scenes.says: Projects add hazards a service call doesn't have. Long shifts, night work, several lifts in one area, material handling, and many circuits in a row. The rules don't change because the work is repetitive. Every circuit locked out and verified live-dead-live before you touch conductors. Every lift inspected every shift. Fatigue is a real hazard. If you're too tired to work safely, say so.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Supervisor on camera in the shop, then cut back to Kyle.
scenes.says: One note. We no longer do group relamping. Older fixtures get LED kits or new fixtures now. The old project lessons still apply, because the planning problems are the same. Same tech, different gear. On a project, you plan the work before you touch it. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.
